stem.text: The function f is continuous for all real x and differentiable for all x except \( x = \frac{15}{2} \), where its graph has a corner. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 3 < c < 12 \), such that \( f'(c) = - \frac{1}{9} \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(12) - f(3)}{12 - 3} = - \frac{1}{9} \), f is not differentiable at \( x = \frac{15}{2} \), which lies in \( (3, 12) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[3, 12\right] \) is \( \frac{f(12) - f(3)}{12 - 3} = \frac{6 - 7}{9} = - \frac{1}{9} \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[3, 12\right] \) and differentiable on \( (3, 12) \), but f is not differentiable at \( x = \frac{15}{2} \), which lies in \( (3, 12) \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = - \frac{1}{9} \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(12) - f(3)}{12 - 3} = - \frac{1}{9} \), the Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be differentiable on \( (3, 12) \).
options.derivation: the Mean Value Theorem applied without checking its hypotheses, which fail at x = 15/2

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(12) - f(3)}{12 - 3} = - \frac{1}{9} \), the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be continuous on \( \left[3, 12\right] \).
options.derivation: the Intermediate Value Theorem cited for a claim about the derivative

options.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(12) - f(3)}{12 - 3} = - \frac{1}{9} \), f is not differentiable at \( x = \frac{15}{2} \), which lies in \( (3, 12) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

Yes. Since \( \frac{f(12) - f(3)}{12 - 3} = - \frac{1}{9} \), there is a c with \( 3 < c < 12 \) and \( f'(c) = - \frac{1}{9} \), because an average rate of change is always reached by the derivative.
options.derivation: existence asserted from the arithmetic alone, with no theorem named and no check that one applies
